entities.name: Holstein-Gottorp-Romanov
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Holstein-Gottorp-Romanov dynasty, the German-origin branch of the Russian imperial family that began when Peter III (grandson of Peter the Great through the female line, but a German Holstein-Gottorp prince) briefly ruled Russia (1762) before being deposed by his wife Catherine the Great, continued the Romanov name while introducing German blood — so thoroughly that by 1917, Nicholas II's actual biological connection to the original Romanovs was minimal. The Holstein-Gottorp-Romanovs governed Russia from 1762 to 1917 — the dynasty's most consequential century — through Catherine the Great's Enlightenment absolutism, Napoleon's defeat, Alexander II's emancipation of serfs, and Nicholas II's catastrophic WWI leadership.

The key rulers: Catherine the Great (r. 1762-1796), herself a German princess of Anhalt-Zerbst who had Peter III murdered/deposed, expanded Russia to the Black Sea, partitioned Poland three times (creating the 'Jewish Pale of Settlement'), and presided over Russia's cultural flowering while maintaining rigid serfdom. Alexander II (r. 1855-1881) — the 'Tsar Liberator' — emancipated Russia's 23 million serfs (1861), the largest emancipation in world history; he was assassinated by socialist revolutionaries (March 13, 1881) on the day he was to sign a proto-constitutional reform.

Nicholas II (r. 1894-1917) — the dynasty's last ruler — was fundamentally unsuited for the challenges of modern governance: he resisted constitutional reform until 1905 (when the Revolution forced him to create the Duma), mismanaged WWI through personal command, and failed to address food shortages and military mutinies. His abdication (March 15, 1917) and execution with his family at Yekaterinburg (July 17, 1918) ended the dynasty. The Holstein-Gottorp-Romanov era — from Catherine the Great's expansion to Nicholas II's collapse — is Russia's defining political century.
